title: Habits and truths: the aorist
intro: This unit adds the aorist (*geniş zaman*, literally **the broad tense**): *Her sabah çay içerim* (I drink tea every morning). It is the tense of habits and general truths, and of offers, requests and promises made on the spot: *Çay içer misiniz?* (Would you like some tea?), *Yarın ararım* (I'll call tomorrow). Its forms take some learning: the vowel of the suffix depends on the verb, thirteen common verbs break the rule, and the negative has a shape of its own.

sections.title: Okur, yapar, çalışır: the forms of the aorist

blocks.text: The aorist is built like the present continuous and the future: the stem, the tense suffix, and the type I endings of **to be** (see [the two sets](gp-person-endings-types)). What changes from verb to verb is the suffix itself, which has three shapes. The stem decides which one it takes.
**After a vowel: `-r`.** *oku-* → *okur*, *bekle-* → *bekler*, *anla-* → *anlar*, *yürü-* → *yürür*. The stem stays as it is, *de-* and *ye-* included: *der* (says), *yer* (eats).

**A one-syllable stem ending in a consonant: `-Ar`**, with two-way harmony: *yap-* → *yapar*, *iç-* → *içer*, *yaz-* → *yazar*, *sev-* → *sever*, *bak-* → *bakar*. *Git-* and *et-* soften before the vowel, as with `-(I)yor` and the future: *gider*, *eder*, and every phrase with *etmek*: *yardım eder*, *dans eder*. Thirteen one-syllable verbs take `-Ir` instead: they are the next section.
**A stem of two or more syllables ending in a consonant: `-Ir`**, with four-way harmony: *çalış-* → *çalışır*, *öğren-* → *öğrenir*, *otur-* → *oturur*, *getir-* → *getirir*, *konuş-* → *konuşur*.

items.en: I drink tea every morning.
Ayşe reads a lot of books.
My father cooks at the weekend.
We usually go to work by bus.
Cats like fish.
Children wake up early.

blocks.text: The vowel changes of `-(I)yor` don't apply here: *bekler*, *anlar*, *der*, *yer* keep their vowel (compare *bekliyor*, *anlıyor*, *diyor*, *yiyor*). And **two or more** counts the syllables of the stem, not of the infinitive: *yap-mak* has a one-syllable stem, so *yapar*; *çalış-mak* has two, so *çalışır*.
Because the aorist can't always be predicted, dictionaries give it for every verb, and so do [the flashcards](cards) of this course: *gitmek, gider*; *almak, alır*.

Thirteen common one-syllable verbs take `-Ir`, not `-Ar`. Nothing in their shape tells you so: learn them as a list. They are some of the most frequent verbs in the language, so you will hear them all the time.

blocks.text: Compare them with regular verbs that look alike: *gelir* but *girer* (enters), *alır* but *açar* (opens), *bulur* but *koyar* (puts), *verir* but *sever*, *görür* but *döner* (returns). Phrases built on one of the thirteen follow it: *duş almak* → *duş alır*, *geç kalmak* → *geç kalır*, *memnun olmak* → *memnun olur*.

items.en: The bus comes at eight every morning.

items.tr: Annem ekmeği her zaman fırından alır.
items.seg: Annem ekmeği her zaman fırından al|ır.
items.en: My mother always buys the bread at the bakery.
We usually stay at home at the weekend.
The train arrives in Ankara in the evening.
I think Elif will come tomorrow.

blocks.text: *Sanırım* (I think, I suppose) is one of the most frequent aorists of all, and a good way to soften a statement: *Sanırım yağmur yağacak* (I think it's going to rain).
The thirteen are irregular only in the positive. Their negatives follow the rule of the next section like every other verb: *gelmez*, *almaz*, *bilmez*.

sections.title: Gelmem, gelir misin? Negative and questions

blocks.text: **Negative.** The negative aorist is `-mAz`, the same for every verb. For **I** and **we** the z disappears: *gelmem* (I don't come), and *gelmeyiz* (we don't come), with a buffer y before *-iz*. The other persons keep it: *gelmezsin, gelmez, gelmezsiniz, gelmezler*.

**Questions.** The aorist takes type I endings, so in a question the ending moves onto `mI`, which follows the vowel of the suffix: *Gelir misin?* (Do you come? Will you come?), *Yapar mısınız?* For **they**, *-lAr* stays on the verb: *Gelirler mi?* The negative question is built on `-mAz`: *Gelmez misin?* (Don't you come? Won't you come?)

blocks.caption: A second verb: *yapmak* (to do), with back vowels
head: Person
Positive
Negative
Question

items.en: I don't drink coffee.
Elif never eats meat.
We're never late.
Does this bus go to Taksim?
Don't you work on Sundays?
Do you like fish?

blocks.text: **I don't** is *-mAm*, never *-mAzım*: *gelmem*, *yapmam*. **We don't** is *-mAyIz*: *gelmeyiz*, *yapmayız*. And the negative doesn't soften the stem, because `-mAz` starts with a consonant: *gitmez*, *kaybetmez*.
*Bilmem* (I don't know, I wouldn't know) is a casual answer, a little vaguer than *Bilmiyorum*: *Ali nerede? — Bilmem.*
The aorist is **broad**: it doesn't describe one moment but what is usually, generally or always so. Four uses cover most of what you will hear.

items: **Habits**, often with a frequency word: *Her sabah yedide kalkarım* (I get up at seven every morning), *Bazen yürürüm* (Sometimes I walk).
**General truths and descriptions**: *Kediler balık sever* (Cats like fish), *Bu otobüs Kadıköy'e gider* (This bus goes to Kadıköy).

**Offers and polite requests**, as questions: *Çay içer misiniz?* (Would you like some tea?), *Kapıyı açar mısın?* (Could you open the door?), *Bakar mısınız?* (Excuse me!, to a waiter or a shop assistant: literally **will you look?**).
**Promises, decisions and guesses made on the spot**: *Merak etme, yarın ararım* (Don't worry, I'll call tomorrow), *Ben bir çay alırım* (I'll have a tea), *Herhâlde gelir* (He'll probably come).

blocks.text: **Aorist or present continuous?** `-(I)yor` says what is going on now or these days: *Ne yapıyorsun?* (What are you doing?). The aorist says what is true in general. In everyday speech `-(I)yor` also covers habits, so *Her sabah koşuyorum* is as natural as *Her sabah koşarım*; the aorist sounds more timeless, like a description of who you are.

**Aorist or future?** For a promise or a decision made as you speak, the aorist is the natural choice: *Seni ararım* (I'll call you). The future of [unit 3](gp-future) states a plan: *Seni yarın arayacağım* (I'm going to call you tomorrow).

blocks.text: *Hiç* and *asla* need a negative verb: *Hiç et yemem* (I never eat meat), *Asla geç kalmam* (I'm never late). *Asla* is the stronger of the two. There is more on *hiç* in [unit 5](gp-negative-polarity).

items.en: I get up at seven every morning.
Excuse me, the bill please.
Could you open the door?
Don't worry, I'll call you tomorrow.

items.tr: Ne içersiniz? — Ben bir çay alırım.
items.seg: Ne iç|er|siniz? — Ben bir çay al|ır|ım.
items.en: What will you have? — I'll have a tea.
He'll probably come this evening.

blocks.text: *Olur* (it will do, literally **it becomes**) means **OK, fine, sure**, and *Olmaz* means **no way**, **that won't do**: *Yarın gelir misin? — Olur.* *Ne dersin?* (What do you say? What do you think?) is the aorist of *demek*.

You have been using the aorist since the first unit. *Teşekkür ederim* and *rica ederim* are aorists of *etmek*, *özür dilerim* of *dilemek* (to wish for), *görüşürüz* (see you) of *görüşmek* (to see each other).

English separates **I drink tea** from **I'm drinking tea**, and so does Turkish: *Çay içerim*, *Çay içiyorum*. But the Turkish offer *Çay içer misiniz?* is closer to **Would you like some tea?** than to **Do you drink tea?** French uses its present for both: je bois du thé, vous prenez un thé ?

summary: Aorist: stem + `-r` after a vowel (*okur*), `-Ar` after a one-syllable stem (*yapar*, *içer*), `-Ir` after a longer stem (*çalışır*), then type I endings: *içerim, içersin, içer*.
Thirteen one-syllable verbs take `-Ir`: *alır, bilir, bulur, durur, gelir, görür, kalır, olur, ölür, sanır, varır, verir, vurur*.
Negative `-mAz`, with *-mAm* for **I** and *-mAyIz* for **we**: *gelmem, gelmezsin, gelmez, gelmeyiz*. The thirteen are regular here.
Questions move the ending onto `mI`: *Gelir misin?*, *Gelmez misin?*, but *Gelirler mi?*
Uses: habits (*Her sabah koşarım*), general truths (*Kediler balık sever*), offers and requests (*Çay içer misiniz?*, *Bakar mısınız?*), promises on the spot (*Yarın ararım*).
*Hiç* and *asla* with a negative verb mean **never**: *Hiç et yemem*.
Set phrases: *Olur* (OK), *Olmaz* (no way), *Bilmem* (I don't know), *Sanırım* (I think), *Ne dersin?* (What do you think?).
